newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Board rejects move against Conrail/CSX merger.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Board rejects move against Conrail/CSX merger.

text.p: The U.S. Surface Transportation Board Thursday rejected a request by Norfolk Southern Corp to overrule a provision of Conrail Inc's merger deal with CSX Corp.
The so-called lockout, or exclusivity, provision of the merger agreement prevents Conrail from seeking another merger partner before 1999.
"We find that Norfolk Southern's petition for relief is premature and unwarranted at this time," the board's decision said.
Earlier this month, Conrail and CSX extended the lockout period from an earlier cut-off date of July 1997.

"While the now two-year lockout period appears excessive on its face, we do not find the extended termination date, in and of itself, to be unreasonable at this time, given the complicated and controversial matters facing the parties," the board said.

The board, which oversees railroads, also rejected Norfolk Southern's arguments that, under the provision, CSX would unlawfully control Conrail because the lockout would remain in effect even if Conrail shareholders vote against the merger.
"Conrail has pointed out ... that Norfolk Southern's case is founded on the uncertainty of future events, rather than on any actual controversy or complaint, and we agree," it said.
The board also rejected concerns that CSX could use the lockout provision to coerce Conrail shareholders in a January 17 vote, saying the shareholders were aware of their options.
However, the board advised that if a CSX/Conrail merger application is filed, it may exercise its powers to impose certain conditions on the deal.

A federal court in Philadelphia was also considering Norfolk Southern's request Thursday. Norfolk Southern lost a court battle in November in which it challenged previous terms of the deal, including the earlier lockout provision.
Norfolk Southern is pursuing a $115-a-share, $10.3 billion bid for Conrail, which has agreed to merge with CSX in a deal worth more than $9 billion.
